title: A bot shopping at the station never mirrors the player's ready
description:
Reported from a nightly run: an engineer beside spawn who never pressed F4,
while a player on RED had.

## Cause

`UpdateDefenderReadiness` says of itself, at
`source/redbots3/nextbot_behavior.sp:762`:

> Several places set a bot ready and gating each of them would be four chances
> to miss one, so this takes the ready away again while the nest is unfinished,
> **every frame, wherever it came from.**

It did not run every frame. `CTFBotTacticalMonitor_Update` returns early for a
bot standing in the upgrade zone with a `DefenderUpgrade` action, and that
return sat above the readiness call. So a bot shopping at the station had no
readiness of its own at all. Only the upgrade action's own exits set it, and the
human-mirror never applied to it.

The mirror is the half that matters here. With a player on RED the bots are
supposed to follow him:

    if (AnyHumanOnRed())
        SetPlayerReady(actor, AnyHumanReadyOnRed());

A bot that never reaches that line does not follow anybody. The upgrade station
on Decoy is beside spawn, which is where the engineer was standing.

## Fix

The readiness update now runs before the early returns, which is what the
comment already claimed. `SetPlayerReady` no-ops when the flag already agrees,
so running it on more frames costs nothing on the wire.

`READY_GRACE` is 90 seconds and only ever forces ready, so starting its deadline
during shopping cannot hold a wave that would otherwise have started.

## If it recurs

This is the mechanism found and fixed, not a confirmed reproduction of that
exact engineer. If a bot is seen unready beside spawn again, it is a different
path, and the thing to capture is whether he was inside the upgrade zone.
close_reason: Fixed. UpdateDefenderReadiness moved above the upgrade-zone early return in CTFBotTacticalMonitor_Update, which is what its own comment already claimed. Compiles clean, warning count unchanged at 54.

title: Decoy ships with no sniper spots, left over from a test
description:
`configs/defenderbots/map/mvm_decoy.cfg` carries this, and nothing else where
the spots used to be:

    //TEMPORARILY REMOVED FOR A TEST

The `SniperSpot` block held six origins. Commit 5aedaff, "a sniper with no spot
fights, and the test-bed counts duplicate buildings", took them out to test the
no-spot path. They were never put back.

## It is in the shipped tag

`v2.15.0` is what `DEFENDERBOTS_VERSION` names and what the nightly builds, and
`git show v2.15.0:configs/defenderbots/map/mvm_decoy.cfg` has no `SniperSpot`
section at all. So every nightly run of Decoy plays with zero sniper spots.

The regression is visible in one line of the server console. Cowser's v1.9.0
bundle logged:

    Config_LoadMap: mvm_decoy: 6 sniper, 3 nest, 0 nest-tank, 0 nest-notank,
    3 dispenser, 0 tele-in, 1 tele-out

A current run should log `0 sniper` on the same map.

## Fix

Restore the six origins from 5aedaff and delete the comment. They are in the
history, so this is a revert of that hunk rather than a re-survey:

    git show 5aedaff -- configs/defenderbots/map/mvm_decoy.cfg

Then check the other map configs for the same thing. One test comment left in
one file is a habit, not an accident, and `Config_LoadMap` prints a count for
every category on every map, so a sweep of the counts against the configs finds
any others cheaply.

Worth adding a test that fails when a map config carries a "TEMPORARILY" or
"TODO" marker, or when a category the map is expected to have comes back zero.
The line that would have caught this was already being printed and nobody was
reading it.
close_reason: Fixed in e20deb3. The six SniperSpot origins are restored from 5aedaff and the TEMPORARILY REMOVED comment is gone. Config_LoadMap should read 6 sniper on Decoy again. Swept every other map config: no other leftover test marker. Community maps have no nests, dispensers or teleporters at all, which is incomplete surveying rather than a leftover, and is not this bead.

title: Bots ignore the tank, and a bad lineup cannot kill it
description:
k-kaneta, playing 1.9.0:

> Tank seems a bit problematic? some bot doesn't really care about tank, and bad
> team comp can make some tank unkillable possibly

Two separate faults, and the second is the one that ends runs.

## Bots do not target the tank

Some bots carry on with the robot wave while the tank rolls past. The tank is a
different kind of target: it does not shoot back, it never stops, and ignoring
it costs the mission rather than the fight in front of you.

Find what the bot AI treats as a threat and check whether the tank is in it at
all. A tank that is never a target explains "doesn't really care" exactly.

## A lineup that cannot out-damage it

The worse half. A tank has a fixed health pool and a fixed time to reach the
hatch, so there is a damage-per-second floor below which it simply arrives. A
lineup with no burst — the reason a Demoman or a Heavy is usually there — sits
under that floor, and no amount of playing well moves it.

This overlaps mvm-lfh (the Demoman is the weakest seat and is in every lineup)
from the other side: that bead asks whether the seat earns its place, this one
finds the case where the lineup needs it and does not have it.

Two things worth having, in order:

1. Bots target the tank when one is on the map, and weight it by how close it
   is to the hatch. A tank at the last stretch outranks anything else alive.
2. The lineup accounts for it. If the mission has tank waves and the chosen
   comp has no burst damage, either the comp changes or the run says so before
   the wave rather than after the loss.

## Test

Decoy has tank waves and is what the playtesters are on. Run it with a
deliberately poor lineup (the all-Scout case the config already allows via
`srcds_bot_team_comp`) and confirm both that the bots shoot the tank and that
the wave is winnable.
design:
## Prior art, and the cause of the first half

Read against Source SDK 2013, which carries the whole TF bot tree officially.
Read it, never copy it: its licence requires derivatives stay free and ship
Valve's LICENSE, and this repo does not even have a LICENSE file of its own yet.

The tank is not invisible to the engine's threat model. `CTFBaseBoss` is
declared `: public NextBotCombatCharacter`, and Valve's
`src/game/server/tf/bot/tf_bot_vision.cpp` collects other NextBots alongside
players when it gathers potentially visible entities. So a tank is a thing a
TFBot can see.

The gap is ours, and it is simpler than "doesn't weight the tank properly".
Every threat scan in `source/redbots3/nextbot_behavior.sp` is a
`for (int i = 1; i <= MaxClients; i++)` loop over player slots. A tank is the
entity `tank_boss`, which holds no player slot, so it is outside every one of
those loops. Nothing rejects the tank as a target; nothing ever offers it as
one.

That explains the shape of the report exactly. k-kaneta said *some* bots ignore
the tank, not all of them, and the exception is the Demoman:
`source/redbots3/demoman_stickies.sp` has bespoke tank handling
(`STICKY_TANK_RANGE`, `FEATURE_DEMO_TANK_PIPES`). One class was taught about
tanks by hand and the rest were not.

`tank_boss` appears twice more and neither is targeting:
`nextbot_behavior.sp:1697` is a path-obstruction filter, and `dbtm.sp` counts
spawns.

So the fix is not a weighting change. Threat selection has to be able to
consider a non-player entity at all, which is a wider change than it looks:
every scan assumes a client index. Decide whether the tank becomes a synthetic
threat those loops can carry, or whether tank targeting sits beside them as its
own pass.

For the second half, the damage floor, `src/game/server/tf/player_vs_environment/
tf_base_boss.h` has the accessors that set the sum: initial health and max
speed. Health over the time it takes to walk its path is the DPS a lineup has
to beat.

title: The red team caps at six, and raising it stops bots spawning
description:
Blabber:

"is it possible to fill red team up more than 6?"
"the bots are really dumb so i'd like to add more but the max player count is 6"
"i tried changing the number to 12 but then it stops adding bots"

Two separate things, and the second is ours.

MvM is built around a six-slot red team: tf_mvm_defenders_team_size, the
upgrade station, the ready-up panel and the scoreboard all assume it. Raising
it is a game-side question and may not be winnable.

But raising it silently breaks us rather than refusing: the bots stop being
added at all, so a player who tries twelve ends up with fewer bots than they
had at six. Whatever the real ceiling is, find it, clamp to it, and log the
clamp. Failing loudly at seven beats spawning nothing at twelve.

First job is to reproduce: set the size to 12 on a testbed run and find where
the add path gives up (slot allocation, the team assign, or the ready gate).
design:
## Cause

Nothing in this mod ever wrote `tf_mvm_defenders_team_size`.
`sm_redbots_manager_defender_team_size` was raised to twelve, twelve bots were
asked for with `tf_bot_add ... red`, and the game went on refusing RED past its
own six. The bots went nowhere and nothing said why, which is the "stops adding
bots" in the report.

There is a second disagreement worth knowing about. The Archipelago plugin
reads the *game's* convar for its own fill and trim
(`tf2_archipelago/bots.inc`, `DefenderTeamSize`). So on a server running both,
a mod set to twelve and a game left at six had the plugin actively trimming RED
back to six while the mod tried to fill it. They now agree, because the mod
writes the game's number.

## What was changed

`ConVarChanged_DefenderTeamSize` writes the wanted number to
`tf_mvm_defenders_team_size`, reads it back, and clamps itself to what stuck.
The ceiling is therefore the game's answer at runtime rather than a constant
guessed here, and every call site keeps reading one convar and gets a number the
game will honour. The clamp is logged and announced in chat.

The convar also gained bounds and a description. It had neither.

## Still to do: the reproduction the bead asked for

Whether the game accepts more than six is not answered by this. The code asks
and obeys, which is correct either way, but nobody has yet run the testbed with
the size at twelve to see what `tf_mvm_defenders_team_size` reads back as.

That run is the remaining work, and it decides whether this is now "twelve bots
work" or "the game refuses and says so". Either is an improvement on twelve
bots silently becoming none.

title: Bots spy-check the human player and each other
description:
SwagDoll420: "another bug I found is that when playing as Spy, your teammates keep
trying to call you out as an enemy spy. They also keep trying to Spycheck each
other, and it keeps screwing me over."

Two symptoms in one report:

1. The bots call out the human player as an enemy Spy when he plays Spy.
2. The bots spy-check each other, and the shooting costs the player his run.

Not diagnosed. What the code does today, as a place to start rather than as a
cause: `behavior/spycheck.sp:222` and `:240` pick suspects from the actor's own
team, and neither line filters out a real player. `nextbot_behavior.sp:1034`
suspends the running action for `CTFBotSpyCheck` when it is possible.

The obvious fix is not obviously right. A disguised enemy Spy is meant to look
like a teammate, so a rule that says "never suspect a teammate" removes spy
checking altogether. The discriminator has to separate a human on RED from a
BLU Spy who appears to be on RED, and whether `TF2_GetClientTeam` already
reports the true team rather than the disguise decides how much work that is.

The paranoia behaviour shipped since 1.3: "Spy checking: paranoia from the last
sighting, suspect the teammate who was not there a moment ago." A human player
who moves differently from the bots fits that description every time.
close_reason:
Fixed and measured, and both halves of the report were the same cause.

The sighting rule in Event_PlayerDeath was 'a Spy killed somebody on another team', which a defending Spy satisfies every time he stabs a robot. So the player's own Spy put his whole team on alert, which is why this only happens when somebody plays Spy. A sighting is now a robot's Spy.

The suspect finder also skipped no humans, so a player could be picked as the disguised one. Every robot in this mode is a fake client, so a real player on RED cannot be an enemy Spy. The price is a human on BLU via the mod's join-blue command being unstabbable, which is smaller than a Spy player being frisked by his own team.

Measured with a friendly Spy in the lineup: 187 of 3443 samples spy checking before, 0 of 1676 after. Two lineups without a Spy spent 0 of 8273 samples spy checking, so the trigger was never an actual robot Spy. Firing with a teammate in the crosshair is unchanged at 15 to 18 per cent, which is bots shooting past one another rather than at them, and harmless with friendly fire off.

title: Change bot classes and loadouts mid-mission
description:
Asked independently by two people.

SwagDoll420: "Are you able to switch the bot's classes in between waves?"
CaptPurpleHeart: "is there a way to change the bots mid-mission?"

omaewh4: "Change what? classes and loadouts? It's not here yet".
notes:
Asked a third time, and this one gives the reason.

Swagdoll: "I really wish it was possible to change the bot's classes mid wave,
it would be really useful for when the best bot counters are different for
certain waves"

That is the case for the feature. It is not convenience, it is that a lineup
picked for wave 1 is the wrong lineup for wave 5, and the player has no move to
make about it short of restarting the mission. Note he says mid *wave*, not
between waves like the earlier two asks; between waves is the cheaper half and
probably where this starts.

Third independent request, so P3 -> P2.
The shape it should take, decided.

## Where it lives

A Bots tab in the launcher window, between Session and Log. The tab is only
populated when a server is running; with nothing up it stays empty rather than
showing dead selects. Tab order matters for the same reason the existing comment
in gui_windows.go gives: the run first, then what you do to it, then the log
last, because the log is for when something is wrong.

Note this is a cross-repo bead. The widgets are in tf2-archipelago
(launcher/internal/gui), the behaviour is here.

The picker already exists and is pre-launch only: botTeamPicks and botTeamFrom
in launcher/internal/gui/botteam.go, seat class plus seat loadout, feeding
settings.BotTeam. The live tab is the same widgets with an Apply button instead
of a save, so this is mostly a matter of reusing botteam.go rather than writing
a second picker. Loadouts change live in the same tab; a loadout swap and a
class swap are the same round trip.

Apply writes sm_redbots_manager_team_composition over rcon and tells the mod to
reseat. Nothing new in the protocol.

## The part that is not the GUI

Bots that change class are despawned and respawned, and they lose everything
they bought. On the way back in they must have the money they have earned, and
they must spend it.

Today the respawn path in events.sp sets:

    TF2_SetCurrency(data, GetStartingCurrency(g_iPopulationManager)
                          + GetAcquiredCreditsOfAllWaves())

That is the game's own wave accounting and it is right as far as it goes. It
misses Archipelago money, and it misses it everywhere, not only here:
MvM_GrantCredits in the AP plugin's mvm.inc pays each live player a Cash Bundle,
and MvM_IsPlayer is `!IsFakeClient(client)`. Bots have never received a single
Cash Bundle. 200 credits each, and the team the player is relying on never sees
any of it.

So the respawn number is starting, plus acquired across all waves, plus every
Cash Bundle the run has been granted. The third term does not exist yet in any
running total, because a bundle is a one-shot drop at the moment it lands. It
needs to be counted and kept somewhere both sides can read.

Then they buy: on respawn the bot runs the full upgrade pass and spends down to
what it can no longer afford, rather than trickling purchases over the next
wave. A class swap between waves that leaves six unupgraded bots on the field is
worse than not swapping.

## What to check when it is done

Swap the whole team mid-mission on wave 5 and confirm each bot's currency
matches a human's in the same run to the credit, and that the upgrade pass has
spent it before the wave starts.
The money half of this bead is done, so a mid-mission class change no longer has
to solve it.

A bot that is despawned and respawned as another class comes back through the
join path, and that path used to set currency from the game's own record alone:
starting currency plus credits acquired across the waves. Neither term has ever
seen a Cash Bundle, so every reseat threw the team's Archipelago money away.

It now goes through SetCurrencyWithBundles in redbots3/archipelago.sp, which
adds what the Archipelago plugin says it has paid. Optional native, zero on a
server without the plugin, rechecked whenever a library comes or goes.

What is left on this bead is the part that was always the work: the tab, the
selects, the apply, and the bots buying everything they can afford on the way
back in. The number they buy with is now right.
close_reason: Built and shipped in v2.18.1: the lineup changes on a running mission from the Bot Switcher tab in both interfaces, from the settings save, and from !ap bots. Money survives it, measured on a live server. Documented in both languages. What is left is a play-test with a human on RED, filed separately, because that is confirmation rather than work.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
Where it has to be reachable from, decided in the session of 2026-08-26:

- The `!ap` menu in the game, so a player switching a lineup between waves never
  leaves the server.
- A tab on the launcher's home page, in the window and in the terminal both,
  named "Bot Switcher", sitting between the mission list and the log. Not a
  second editor: the same seats, and an Apply that reaches the running server.

Both interfaces have to read well: columns lined up, and the seats the mod draws
named as such rather than left blank.

And the constraint that decides the mechanism: the bots must not lose money
across a switch. That is what makes a kick-and-rejoin viable at all, because the
join path already sets currency through SetCurrencyWithBundles. It is to be

again, so a change that moves no class still has to reach every bot.
sm_dump_credits is the instrumentation for the money question.

  Reseat: the lineup wants 4 seat(s) nobody holds, kicked 4 bot(s) for them
  Fill: asked for 4, RED holds 2 of 6
  Fill: the named team filled 4 of 4

whose class the new list still wanted and replaced the other four, and the
mid-wave change deferred rather than tearing the team apart.

already live on the Bots page of the settings.

title: Engineer upgrade priority puts the PDA behind weapons and resistances
description:
EZKSupernova, who traced most of his losses to it:

"I think it should be set so the Engi fully upgrades the PDA (but not disposable
mini because that sucks) before even touching his other weapons or his
resistances. Very nearly all of my wave failures have been because the Engi
wasn't pulling his weight. I'm on Wave 6 rn and there's no building health, no
sentry firing speed, no metal capacity, all of which are mandatory upgrades."

He names three he considers mandatory and one to skip: building health, sentry
firing speed, metal capacity; not disposable mini-sentry.
design:
## Confirmed in play, and the line is found

Reported again from a nightly run of Decoy: "they always buy their mini sentry."
That is the same complaint EZKSupernova made, from a second player
independently, so the behaviour is real and repeatable rather than one bad run.

`source/redbots3/behavior/upgrade.sp`, in the `TFClass_Engineer` case, ranks:

    engy dispenser radius increased   330
    engy sentry fire rate increased   320
    engy disposable sentries          310
    engy building health bonus        260
    metal regen                       220
    maxammo metal increased           210

So the disposable mini is bought **third**, ahead of two of the three upgrades
EZK called mandatory. He asked for building health, sentry firing speed and
metal capacity, and explicitly not the mini. Sentry fire rate already outranks
it; building health and metal capacity do not.

That is the whole of "they always buy their mini sentry": at 310 it is bought
on nearly every run, before the nest is durable.

## The value is deliberate, so this is a decision and not a defect

The comment above the line explains why it is 310 rather than absent. The
upgrade was refused for a long time because nothing in the mod placed the second
building, so the game dropped it wherever the engineer faced and the result was
"minis pointing at walls". `behavior/engineerbuilddisposable.sp` now stands it
beside the real one, on ground that sees what the real one sees, and the
promotion followed that work.

The file also states the rule for changing it:

> Measured beats read. If the ordering is to change it should change because a
> run said so, not because a page did.

Two player reports are runs, not pages. But they are reports of what was bought,
not measurements of what it cost, and the credits that go into a mini are
credits that did not go into building health.

## What settles it

The testbed already does A/B runs; `testbed/results/` holds several. Run the
same missions with `engy disposable sentries` at 310 and at something under
`maxammo metal increased`, and compare waves cleared and sentry uptime. That is
the same shape of evidence that put the value at 310, so it can move it.

If the A/B is close, prefer the players. Two independent reports of the same
purchase feeling wrong is worth more than a result inside the noise, and the
mod has demoted an upgrade on that basis before.

One thing to check while there: whether the mini is worth more on a map with
several nests than on Decoy, which has three. If the answer is map-dependent the
priority may want to read the nest count rather than being one number.
close_reason: Measured and acted on. Six waves of Decoy per arm, same build, only sm_redbots_feature_engineer_disposable moved. Defender deaths per wave: off [0,3,5,7,9,10] against on [11,12,14,15,15,17], so the spreads do not touch and the worst wave without the mini beat the best wave with it. Sentries lost 7 against 14, robots killed 73 against 36.5 median, waves cleared 3 of 6 against 2 of 6. The switch now ships off, which is what EZKSupernova asked for. Caveats: one map, six waves an arm, and the arms ran under different machine load; deaths are far less load-sensitive than durations and the separation is total, but a second map is worth running. The rest of his ask, PDA before weapons and resistances, is untouched and belongs in its own bead if it is still wanted.

title: The engineer walks around holding a building and never puts it down
description:
Reported from play on Coal Town, mid wave and between waves both, and the mid
wave one costs the team its sentry for the whole wave.

The carry has no clock. `CTFBotMvMEngineerIdle_Update` only tries to place while
the engineer is within seventy units of the nest centre, so a centre he cannot
reach, or a spot whose placement keeps being refused, leaves him holding it with
nothing in the code to end it. The relocation path has a deadline of its own and
relocation ships off, so nothing else covers it.

`CARRY_GIVE_UP_TIME` is 25 seconds. When it runs out the nest becomes the ground
under his feet, which is what the relocation timeout already does, and the
placing branch below puts it down on the next update.

Not reproduced on the test-bed, and that is worth saying plainly: an engineer
only carries when a sentry buster makes him haul or when a nest moves, and
neither happened in eight waves of Coal Town with relocation on. The fix is from
reading the code against the report rather than from a measurement. The line it
writes is how the next report gets confirmed or denied:

    [defenderbots] carry failed for <name> at <time>: held it too long, putting it down here

Six waves of Coal Town with the clock in and relocation on, five cleared and no
crash, so it costs nothing where it does not fire.
close_reason: Fixed in a87d742: CARRY_GIVE_UP_TIME is 25 seconds, after which the nest becomes the ground under his feet. Not reproduced on the test-bed, so the log line it writes is how the next report is confirmed. Six waves of Coal Town with it in, five cleared, no crash.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text: More evidence from the video, and it is the same root as mvm-oh7: while stuck he was scrolling through his weapons and opening and cancelling the build menu. That is two paths undoing each other every frame - the carry logic equipping the wrench and pressing fire to place, and the build gate equipping the toolbox and reopening the menu because it saw no sentry. The gates count a carried building now, which removes the trigger; the 25 second carry clock stays as the backstop.

title: The Gas Passer crashed the server
description:
A Pyro carrying a Gas Passer trips the watchdog at a wave transition:

```
WatchDog! Server took too long to process (probably infinite loop).
FATAL ERROR: Host_Error: WatchdogHandler called - server exiting.
```

Four runs in six on `mvm_decoy`, and clean six waves running with a shotgun in
that slot instead. It was four in six rather than every run because the forced
lineup has no Pyro in it: `sm_redbots_manager_extra_bots` adds one beyond the
composition and sometimes rolls Pyro.

The fault is here, not in the weapon. `EquipBestWeaponForThreat` says to throw
gas whenever `HasAmmo(secondary)` is true, and `HasAmmo` on a weapon that fires
off a charge meter rather than a clip is always true. So the Pyro equips a jar
it cannot throw, every tick, and never picks the flamethrower back up.

Fixed: `IsThrowableReady` asks the meter instead of the ammo, and the three
places in that switch which reached for `HasAmmo` on a jar now go through it.
The Gas Passer's meter is on the player, per loadout slot, because it fills from
damage dealt; Jarate, Mad Milk and the Cleaver fill on a clock the weapon
carries. Both are read.

The loadout still gives the Pyro a shotgun. Putting the Gas Passer back is a
balance question rather than a crash one now, and the file already says the
airblast it costs is worth measuring rather than assuming.

The Gas Passer is not the whole story. 1.5.5-tf2ap.10, which has no loadout file
at all, crashed twice in three runs of the same mission afterwards, with the same
watchdog line. So there is an intermittent watchdog crash in this mod that
predates all of the above, and the Gas Passer made it far more likely rather than
causing it alone. Rates seen so far, all on `mvm_decoy` with six bots:

| build | crashes |
| --- | --- |
| tf2ap.10 | 2 in 9 |
| this branch, Gas Passer | 4 in 6 |
| this branch, shotgun | 0 in 5 |

The core dumps answered it, and the answer is pathfinding. Backtrace from
core.417, taken with the game copied out of the volume:

```
WatchDogHandler <- Sys_Error <- Host_Error
 <signal handler called>
CTFBotPathCost::operator()
NavAreaBuildPath
Path::Compute
ChasePath::RefreshPath
ChasePath::Update
```

So the frame the watchdog killed was inside path computation, not an infinite
loop in this mod. Anything that asks for a path every tick, for several bots at
once, can push a frame past the watchdog on a machine with nothing spare.

One of those was ours and is fixed: `ConfiguredDispenserSpot` called
`IsPathToVectorPossible` for every configured spot, every tick, per engineer.
The spot is chosen once when the action starts now.

Worth knowing for the next one: `IsPathToVectorPossible` is a full
`NavAreaBuildPath`, and it reads like a cheap predicate.

A sweep of every map found two more of the same shape, and both are fixed:

- An engineer with no sentry answered yes to "should the nest advance", and the
  idle action returns without acting when the answer is yes. So he never
  rebuilt, and every one of those frames ran `PickBuildArea` twice, which calls
  `GetBombInfo`, which walks every nav area on the map. Sixty-six times a
  second, per engineer, for as long as he had no sentry. On Bigrock that was
  most of a wave.
- The tactical monitor asked whether health or ammo was worth walking to on
  every frame for every bot, and the slow path computed a path to every
  candidate. MvM floors are covered in `tf_ammo_pack`. The answer is held for
  half a second now and the search is run for the nearest four candidates
  rather than all of them.

The pattern is worth naming, because it has now produced four separate crashes:
a nav mesh call inside something that reads like a predicate, called from a
per-frame path. Anything asking the mesh a question wants a clock on it.

Item 10 is the fourth, and it came with a symbolised backtrace and a limit:
`PATHS_PER_FRAME` caps the whole team at two path computations a frame. That is
the general answer to this pattern rather than another special case, and the
residual intermittent watchdog crash recorded here should be measured against it
before anything else is tried.

title: The test-bed needs a machine with memory free
description:
Measurement stopped being possible partway through a session, on both builds at
once. 1.5.5-tf2ap.10 played six waves cleanly earlier the same day and then
failed four runs in a row, three of them before a single wave started, with the
watchdog line from item 12. The code did not change between those runs.

What did change is the machine:

```
7.8 GB of memory, around 200 MB free
5.0 GB swapped out
swap-in bursting to 20 MB/s while a run was playing
```

A page fault that stalls the server is indistinguishable, to a watchdog that
measures frame time, from an infinite loop. Running `--no-build` to skip the
per-run image build did not help, so it is the steady state rather than the
build spike.

Two ways out, and they are worth knowing before trusting any number this
test-bed produces: give it a machine with a couple of gigabytes free, or stop
whatever else is running on this one for the duration. What is not worth doing
is reading a crash rate measured under paging as a property of the code, which
is a mistake this file has already recorded once in item 12.

title: Nest relocation trips the server watchdog
description:
`sm_redbots_manager_engineer_nest_relocate` was 0 because turning it on killed
the server at the first wave transition. Reproduced again today on Decoy with two
engineers: the server crashed before a single wave finished.

This time there is a backtrace rather than a guess. The core was read with the
game's own binaries copied out of the container, which is what makes the frames
resolve:

```
WatchDogHandler <- Host_Error <- Sys_Error
 <signal handler called>
CNavArea::GetZ <- CNavArea::ComputePortal
CNavArea::ComputeAdjacentConnectionHeightChange
SMPathFollowerCost::operator()
NavAreaBuildPath (maxPathLength=0)
Path::Compute
natives::nextbot::path::ComputeToPos
 ... SourcePawn JIT frames ...
CHookManager::PlayerRunCmd
CBasePlayer::PhysicsSimulate
```

So the frame the watchdog killed was a nav mesh search, reached from this mod's
own per-frame path refresh inside `PlayerRunCmd`, with no bound on the search.
An unreachable goal makes `NavAreaBuildPath` walk the whole mesh, and six bots
asking in the same frame multiplies it. Relocation makes unreachable goals more
likely, which is why it shows there first and why the same shape has now produced
four crashes.

The fix is a limit rather than a special case. `PATHS_PER_FRAME` is 2: the
per-frame refresh computes at most two paths a frame across the whole team, and
anybody refused tries again next frame. At 66 ticks that is 130 a second against
a refresh that wants one every 0.2 seconds per bot, so nothing waits for a path.
A behaviour that computes once when it starts is never refused, because it has no
retry.

Measured:

| | result |
| --- | --- |
| relocation on, before | crashed before wave 1 finished |
| relocation on, after | 3 waves cleared, then 3 more waves, no crash, no stalls |
| relocation off, after | 2 waves cleared, 206 robots, 17 deaths, 31819 damage |
| relocation off, before | 2 waves cleared, 206 robots, 17 deaths, 32314 damage |

The last two are the regression check: the budget changes nothing about a normal
run.

The convar stays 0. The crash is what kept it off; whether the feature is worth
having is a different question and wants its own measurement.

title: One ask adds twice
description:
`sm_addbots N` runs `AddBotsBasedOnLineupMode(N)`, which calls
`AddBotsFromTeamComposition(N)` first. That added the seats the named team still

`AddBotsFromTeamComposition` returns the count it added now, and the caller

| before | 10 | filled 3 of 6, the lineup mode adds 6 more |
| after | 7 | filled 3 of 6, the lineup mode adds 3 more |

RED is seven rather than six because the test-bed's own host client holds a
seat. Nine bots plus the host is what Peppy reported and what the first run
reproduced.

was kept rather than measured.

title: Bavarian Botbash wave 3 wipes the bot team
description:
Swagdoll: "Bavarian Botbash Wave 3 is still basically impossible for me. That
Giant Crit Heavy and his two Giant Medics keep wiping everything and I'm not good
enough at Sniper to counter it."

Not solved. Six attempts at the wave with nobody on the server, in two
configurations, and all six were lost. What follows is what was measured, what it
ruled out, and the two changes that survived.

**The first three sessions measured the wrong mission.** `tf_mvm_popfile
mvm_rottenburg_advanced_bavarian_botbash` was refused, the server kept playing
Rottenburg's own default, and nothing said so. The real names are in the game's
VPK and there are two: `mvm_rottenburg_advanced1` and `_advanced2`.

```
grep -ao 'mvm_rottenburg[a-z0-9_]*' tf/tf2_misc_dir.vpk
```

`run.sh` reads the popfile back now and stops with the name it is actually
playing, because everything downstream of a silent substitution is fiction.

**A second instrument was lying.** Three of four wave results in a run came out
exactly 2047 characters long: SourceMod's `File.WriteLine` formats through a 2048
byte buffer and the wave result had outgrown it. Truncated JSON is skipped by
every reader, so a four wave run looked like a one wave run. It writes with
`WriteString` now. Any measurement in this file taken on a long line before this
was measuring fewer waves than it thought.

**The uber is not being wasted.** A `uber_held` line is written whenever a
defender dies while a live medic holds a full charge. Over a whole wave 3 there
were none, so the charge is not sitting in his pocket while the team dies.

**The medic's patient churned, and fixing it changed nothing here.** He re-picked
the biggest body every two seconds, and maximum health follows the upgrades the
team buys, so the winner flipped between bodies a few points apart: 18 patient
changes in one wave. A tie keeps the man he has now, `MEDIC_PATIENT_MARGIN`, and
that is 7 changes. The beam is on somebody 27% of the time either way, so the
churn was real and was not what keeps the beam off.

**Where they wait for the wave is worth something on a hard mission and costs on
an easy one.** `MoveToFront` sends everybody to the robots' own gate. Waiting
beside the engineer's sentry instead, three attempts each on the real wave 3:

| | deaths | robots killed | held | distance to a sentry at wave start |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the gate | 22 | 36 | 135s | 823 |
| the nest | 18 | 38 | 127s | 588 |

On Decoy's own mission the same change unconditionally was worse: two waves
cleared and 206 robots killed at the gate, one wave cleared and 165 at the nest.
So the rule is the mission, `hold_the_nest`: meet them at the gate while the team
can afford to, hold the nest when it cannot. Decoy with the rule in place is back
to 206 robots and both waves cleared.

It ships **off**, because it does not clear the bar this file now holds
everything to. Read with the spread beside it, the nest arm's own quartiles are
13 to 23 deaths and they contain the gate arm's median of 22. Four waves an arm
cannot see a difference this size. The switch is there and the measurement that
would settle it is sixteen waves an arm against the baseline band below.

What is still true after all of it: the wave is lost every time, at 18 to 23
defender deaths an attempt. The bots do already shoot robot medics, 56 samples of
it in one wave, so the idea this item started with is in the mod and working.
Nobody has added a balancing knob and nobody should.

The demoknights were the next guess and they were measured too. `ThreatPriority`
ranks a medic, a support class, a giant and a bomb carrier, and a charging
demoknight is none of those: it closes seven hundred and fifty units a second, so
it is outside urgent range until it is inside melee. A `charge_first` rank above
the medic, three attempts: 18 deaths, 39 robots, 119 seconds, against 18, 38 and
127 without it. No effect, and nothing proved the rule ever fired, so it was
reverted rather than shipped as a switch nobody has evidence for.

Two more theories were measured on the real mission and both were wrong.

The engineer spends the wave failing to build. On the real wave 3 he is inside
`DefenderBuildSentrygun` for 24 samples, walking between spots three thousand
units apart, and his sentry is up for half the wave; across the container's life
17 build attempts produced 8 sentries and no give-ups. `PickBuildArea` ranks
spots against the bomb and the bomb moves up the map, and the idle action asks it
again every one to two seconds while he has no sentry.

Holding the nest for the wave instead made it worse: sentry uptime 50% to 29%,
deaths 18 to 22, and the engineer walked further rather than less. The re-picking
is finding him a spot he can actually reach, so the churn is a symptom of spots
that refuse him rather than the cause of the walking.

`IsTankWave` reading live wave icons was the other theory: the game clears icons
as a wave is beaten, so the answer can flip mid-wave, and Rottenburg keeps its
two conditional nests at opposite ends of the map. Caching it for the wave
changed nothing here because wave 3 has no tank in it at all. The reasoning still
holds for a wave that does, and it is worth doing when there is a tank wave to
measure it on.

Spacing was the sixth, and it is the first theory that fitted the deaths: they
are shelled, so standing apart should cost the robots their splash. It worked as
designed and lost anyway. Median distance to the nearest teammate went from 414
units to 564, and deaths went from 18 to 22 with the same robots killed. Spread
out, they lose the medic's beam, each other's fire and the sentry's cover, and a
robot demoman kills them one at a time instead of two at once. Reverted.

The eighth came from the build logging once it worked, and it is the closest any
of them got. Two of five build attempts end with no sentry and none of them end
on a reason the action names, so they are interruptions rather than refusals, and
the trace has the engineer walking to the upgrade station mid-wave with nothing
built. Holding him back from shopping while his nest is down: robots killed 38 to
49, and deaths 18 to 22 with sentry uptime 50% to 41%. He is present and shooting
and his sentry is the one he could not afford to upgrade, so it dies faster.
Reverted, and the trade is worth remembering: an engineer's damage is his sentry
plus himself, and this bought one with the other.

Then the reproduction itself was checked, and it was the wrong question all along.

Playing the real mission from wave 1 rather than jumping into wave 3: the bots
lose **wave 1**, eight attempts out of eight, at 15 to 31 defender deaths each.
Wave 3 is not the wall. This mission is beyond the team from its first wave, and
Swagdoll reaches wave 3 because he is on the server.

Two things were checked along the way and both corrected something believed here:

- Every bot is at stock maximum health in every run on every map, which read like
  a team that never upgrades. It is not: Mann vs Machine sells no maximum health
  upgrade at all. `sm_dump_upgrades` lists the sixty three the game has and there
  is no such line. Stock health is what a human team has too.
- They do shop. The wave line carries `upgrades` now, and a first wave of this
  mission has 28 upgrade steps bought across the team before it starts.
- `--wave` does not grant the credits of the waves it skips, so a jumped wave is
  played by an unupgraded team. That is sound for an A/B, where both arms are
  equally poor, and worthless for "can they win this wave".

Eight attempts at wave 3, eight measurements, and eight losses at wave 1 when the
mission is played properly.

The teleporter is a real defect and neither order fixes it. Over four attempts at
wave 1 there are 116 samples of an entrance standing and 33 of an exit, so most of
the metal goes on the half that moves nobody. Two fixes were measured:

| | entrance | exit | rides | held | deaths a wave |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| entrance first, as shipped | 116 | 33 | 11 | 217s | 32.2 |
| replacing a lost exit mid wave | 31 | 29 | 4 | 166s | 26.5 |
| exit first | 44 | 89 | 15 | 166s | 29.5 |

The pair is complete far more often either way, and both hold the wave for less
time. The engineer finishes one half per break on this map, whichever half he
starts with, because the entrance is a walk to the far end of it. Replacing the
exit mid wave takes him off his sentry, which is the same trade that lost when he
skipped shopping to build: **anything that takes the engineer off his sentry
during a wave shortens the hold.** That is now three measurements saying it.

And a lesson about the measuring rather than the bots: four attempts cannot
resolve a difference in how long a wave is held. The unchanged arm's own
durations are 163, 189, 272 and 241 seconds. Differences of that size between
arms were read here as signal in both directions before the spread was looked at.
Only the state counts are trustworthy at this sample size: 16 attempts at wave 1
across every arm, 16 losses, and a teleporter that is one ended.

The lineup looked like the answer and then did not replicate, which is the most
useful thing measured here.

The map's lineup for Rottenburg names no Pyro, and wave 1 kills the team with
rockets: 62 per cent of the deaths are robot Soldiers and 73 per cent are
explosions. Giving the Scout's seat to a Pyro by hand, eight attempts against
eight: the team held 254 seconds against 176 and killed 88 robots against 58,
which reads as the largest effect anything produced all session.

Then the same lineup was produced by a rule instead of by hand, so that the mod
would field a Pyro whenever the coming wave is explosive, and eight more
attempts came back at 179 seconds and 54 robots. That is the baseline, not the
Pyro arm. Two of the three arms agree and the exciting one is the odd one out,
and its own durations run from 88 to 282 seconds, so it was a lucky sample read
as a discovery. The rule was reverted.

The lesson is the one this file keeps having to learn: an arm that is not
replicated is a story. Eight attempts is enough to see a wave lost sixteen times
out of sixteen and not enough to see a change in how long it is held.

Asked for from play and measured against that band: the classes that fight at
range wait at the engineer's nest and the ones that have to close wait at the
gate, rather than the whole team doing one or the other. Sixteen attempts: 166
seconds held, 25 deaths, 56 robots killed, every one of them inside the
baseline's quartiles. No detectable effect, so `hold_the_nest` stays off and the
switch stays there. It is the first change on this mission that could be called
either way with confidence rather than argued about.

Also asked for from play: a Spy for the big waves. Sixteen attempts with the
Scout's seat given to one, against the same band: 160 seconds held and 25 deaths,
both unchanged, and 44 robots killed against a baseline of 58 whose quartiles are
52 to 64. Outside the band and worse.

The Spy is the top damage dealer on the team while he is doing it, 72102 across
those waves against the Heavy's 62041, and the team still kills a quarter fewer
robots. The seat he took collects the money, and money is upgrades. A class that
does damage is not the same as a seat that is worth having.

There is a baseline band for this wave now, twenty four attempts on the
unchanged build, and it is in `docs/testbed-metrics.md`: 160 seconds held with
quartiles of 154 to 192, 24 deaths with quartiles of 22 to 31, 58 robots killed
with quartiles of 52 to 64, and none of the twenty four cleared. Every future
change to this mission is read against it, and anything whose median lands inside
those quartiles has shown nothing. That is the tool this item needed from the
start.

Money was instrumented properly and then ruled out, and the ruling out included
correcting a reading of my own.

The first version counted what the wave paid and what the team picked up, and the
field for credits spent was declared, printed and never filled. With the whole
life of it counted, dropped, picked up, bonus, spent and still in hand:

- The team collects 78 per cent of what a wave pays out, median over twelve
  waves, as little as 54 per cent of one. That is about 200 credits a wave left
  on the floor.
- It ends a wave holding a median of 3328 credits, which looked like hoarding and
  is not. Forty five shopping trips end with a median of 30 credits in the wallet
  and a range of 0 to 905: they spend what they have. The 3328 is money collected
  during the wave, and the wave is lost before the break that would spend it.
- Thirty five of those forty five trips end on "nothing left worth buying" and
  ten on the game refusing a purchase, which ends the whole trip rather than
  trying the next thing on the list. That last one is worth fixing on its own
  terms and is not worth thousands of credits.

Two changes were measured against the 78 per cent and neither moved it: letting a
bot walk to a pack within 400 units with a threat in sight, and steering the
attack sidestep onto a pack within 600. Both came back at 79 per cent, and an
early three wave read of one of them at 65 per cent was noise, which is the
third time that has happened on this mission and the reason the band exists.

What this item actually is: the bot team is below what an advanced Two Cities
mission asks from its opening wave, and no single behaviour explains it. That is
a programme rather than a bug, and the honest thing to tell the player is that
the bots need him. The measurements above rule out the medic's charge, his
patient, target priority, where the team waits, how spread out it stands, and
whether the engineer shops before building. What is left is a lot of small things
at once, which is what "the bots are not good enough yet" looks like from
inside. What is
left to try, in the order a measurement is cheapest:

- Count what actually kills them by robot class and weapon on this wave rather
  than in the aggregate. `killed us` says pyro and heavy on the wrong mission and
  has not been read for the right one.
- Sentry uptime through the wave: the engineer put 8% of his buildings' damage
  back on the wrong mission, and a nest that is down is a team fighting in the
  open whatever it decided to shoot.
- Whether the team should retreat at all. Nothing in this mod ever gives ground,
  and a wave that walks over a held line is the one case where falling back to
  the next choke is what a person does.

title: One engineer builds two dispensers, reproduced on the testbed
description:
Peppy: "Engineer bots can sometimes build 2 dispensers."

The per-owner building samples walk `TF2Util_GetPlayerObject`, which is the
game's own list and holds one entry per type, so a second dispenser on one
builder is exactly what that list cannot show. A second instrument walks the
entities instead and counts them against `m_hBuilder`.

First run, four waves: two engineers each held two dispensers, for three samples
each. Second run, with entities that are being placed or carried excluded: none
at all, over four waves.

So no engineer ever holds two built dispensers. What he holds is the blueprint,
which is a real `obj_dispenser` with his name on it, while his own dispenser
stands at the nest. That is what a person watching sees as a second one, and it
is why the report says "sometimes".

Both are written down now: a `duplicate` line if a builder ever holds two of a
type, and a `ghost` line for each blueprint or carried building. A three wave run
had eight ghost samples on one engineer, dispenser and sentry, so a blueprint can
be out for the length of a walk across the map.

That is the honest end of this item unless somebody sends a screenshot of two
dispensers standing. If it turns out to be the blueprint that bothers people, the
fix is the engineer cancelling the placement when he stops walking to a spot, and
the `ghost` lines are what would measure it.
design:
## Cause found, and the other candidate is measured out

`listed` answered it. Four waves of Decoy: `held:2 built:2 listed:2`, eighteen
times. `listed` is the count from `TF2Util_GetPlayerObject`, the list every gate
in this mod asks. It agreeing at 2 means the gates could see both buildings, so
nothing was blind and the fix does not belong in `GetObjectOfType`. That branch
is closed.

The real cause is a one-frame race in
`source/redbots3/behavior/engineerbuilddispenser.sp`:

    VS_PressFireButton(actor);                                  // acts next tick
    int dispenser = GetObjectOfType(actor, TFObject_Dispenser);  // asked now
    if (dispenser == INVALID_ENT_REFERENCE)
        return action.Continue();                                // so it presses again

The press puts the building down on the tick after it, so a question asked in
the same frame is always answered "none". The action carried on, the toolbox
re-armed, and it pressed again. Two dispensers, one engineer.

The same trap as `m_bInUpgradeZone` in the refund probe, where the trigger only
sets the property on the next tick.

## Fixed

The check runs before the press and ends the action as soon as a dispenser
exists, so a re-armed toolbox cannot produce a second. A press is also given a
tick to land before another is allowed.

`engineerbuildsentrygun.sp` has the same shape and got the same guard. That one
is **recognised, not measured**: a sentry standing twice under one engineer is
what was reported as three sentries for two engineers, but no run has counted
it.

## Left open until the verification run says zero

Before: 18 duplicates over four waves. After should be none. Not tagged until
that comes back, because a fix for a race deserves the same bar as a weight
change.

One thing still unexplained and worth writing down: TF2 normally allows one
dispenser per engineer. Two standing, finished, with the game's own list
agreeing, means something on the MvM side permitted it. The fix holds whatever
that is, because it stops the second press rather than relying on the game to
refuse, but nobody knows why the game said yes.

The check now runs before the press and ends the action as soon as a dispenser exists, and a press gets a tick to land before another is allowed. Four waves of Decoy: 18 duplicate events before, 0 after, with 138 dispensers and 138 sentries still sampled so the engineers build normally. listed:2 in the before-run ruled out the other candidate: the game's object list saw both, so no gate was blind and the fix did not belong in GetObjectOfType. engineerbuildsentrygun.sp has the same shape and got the same guard, recognised rather than measured. Still unexplained: TF2 normally allows one dispenser per engineer, and why the game permitted a second is unknown; the fix stops the press rather than relying on the game to refuse.

comments.text: Cowser, mid-wave: "it was trying to place a dispenser but just couldn't and gave up for some reason". omaewh4 confirmed: "ahh and you were mid-wave? that happened to me too, but on the start of the wave he just put it normally". comments.text: Original report, Peppy on 1.9.0 release day: "Engineer bots can sometimes build 2 dispensers".

comments.author: m-this
comments.text:
Reopened: my close was wrong. A photograph from play shows two dispensers standing with one engineer who was never kicked or replaced, and my measurement could not have seen it - every run I checked had the engineer never carrying a building, and the world scan excludes anything being placed or carried.

The mechanism is the carry. TF2 removes a building from the player's object list the moment he picks it up, so GetObjectOfType(engineer, dispenser) answers none while he holds one; the gate in CTFBotMvMEngineerIdle_Update then says 'no dispenser, build one', he places a fresh one, and when the carried one goes down there are two.

Ruled out by test rather than argument: kicking an engineer holding a level three dispenser removed the dispenser and left no orphan, so it is not ownership loss.

Fixed by HasObjectOfType, which counts the carried one, used by the dispenser gate and the teleporter's sentry and dispenser checks. Six waves of Coal Town with relocation on: five cleared, no crash, never more than one dispenser at once. It shares a root with the carry having no clock, which is closed separately.

title: Sniper bots on the stock loadout stand in spawn
description:
Peppy, and he said it predates 1.9.0: "Sniper bots with the stock loadout don't
seem to work, they just stay in spawn."

A sniper had never been in a test-bed lineup: 3417 engineer samples in
`results/` and not one sniper, which is why this survived. Forced into one on
Decoy, on the build with item 17 fixed, he works: `SniperLurk` under his stack
for the whole mission, 1970 damage and 14 kills over three waves.

That is the answer. A rifle sniper is one of the classes `ShouldTakeUpPosition`
refuses, so with item 17's stale shopping flag he had no behaviour for the whole
break and stood where he spawned. The same freeze as the engineers, and fixed
with them.

The rest of this item is a fix that was written, measured and thrown away, and
it is worth keeping because the reasoning was sound and the measurement said no.

`SetupSniperSpotHints` takes the team off every `func_tfbot_hint` when the map
config names no `SniperSpot`, and the game's sniping behaviour walks to a hint of
its own team. So on an unconfigured map a rifle sniper looked like he would have
nowhere to go, and the fix was to let him fight instead. Decoy with its
`SniperSpot` block removed, two waves each way:

| | damage | kills | standing still |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| lurking, as shipped | 4521 | 35 | 24 of 63 samples |
| falling back to attacking | 570 | 7 | 11 of 82 samples |

The premise was wrong. The game's lurk finds its own spot without a hint, and a
sniper on his rifle is worth eight times a sniper walking around shooting at
things. The change was reverted. What it did prove is that standing still is what
a sniper is supposed to do, so "he is not moving" is not evidence of a broken
sniper, and the next report of one wants damage per wave beside it.

title: The medic had nothing to do between waves
description:
Left behind by item 17. With the shopping flag fixed the medic still spent three
quarters of the break with no behaviour on his stack.

`ShouldTakeUpPosition` refused four classes, on the reasoning that each has
somewhere else to be: the engineer has his nest, the spy is lurking, the sniper
with a rifle has his spot, and the medic follows a patient. The first three hold.
The medic does not: between rounds he heals nobody, so nothing suspends for him,
and following a patient is not a behaviour he has when there is no healing to do.
His patient is walking to the front, so that is where he goes now.

Measured on the same mission as item 17, two waves, both cleared either way:

| | medic, no behaviour in the break | healing done | defenders died | damage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before | 76% | 876 | 18 | 30922 |
| after | 0% | 1560 | 17 | 32314 |

Every bot on the team is now at 0%. Two waves is too small to call the healing a
win; it is enough to say nothing regressed.

title: Something walks the engineer into the same wedge on Mannworks
description:
The wedge recovery on mvm-hnb moves a stuck bot off the geometry it is inside,
and on Mannworks with Mean Machines it fired four times in four waves. Three of
those were the same coordinates: 1014 885 274.

So the recovery works and the cause does not go away. Something keeps routing
the engineer into one spot he cannot get out of, and the net catches him every
time rather than once.

Worth finding, because a bot that is teleported out mid-wave has still lost the
seconds it spent wedged, and the recovery is a safety net rather than an answer.

Where to look: 1014 885 274 on mvm_mannworks, and what the nest picker offers
that leads him through it. configs/defenderbots/map/mvm_mannworks.cfg holds the
spots.

Related: mvm-ipf and mvm-zx0 are the same shape on other maps and may share the
cause.

title: Nothing records what killed a defender, or how far an upgrade got
description:
mvm-gwq closed on a measurement that also showed what the test-bed cannot see.
Two questions came out of it and neither can be answered today:

- **A resistance is bought, but to what tier?** One tier may not be enough
  against the wave that killed the bot. Nothing logs the level each bot reaches
  on each upgrade, so "they buy it" and "they buy enough of it" are the same
  line in the results.
- **What killed the defender?** testbed/results/ records deaths per wave and
  not their cause. A Scout dying to something a resistance does not cover looks
  exactly like a Scout dying because the resistance was too cheap to buy.

Both are one field each in the wave result. Until they exist, any bead of the
form "the bots do not buy enough X" is unfalsifiable, which is how mvm-gwq sat
at P0 on a premise that turned out to be wrong.

Third thing worth a look while in there: nine of the 38 trips ended with "the
game refused one". The upgrade file says a refusal repeats until the window
closes, so a bot that hits one may be spending less than it could.

title: Play-test the Bot Switcher with somebody on RED
description:
mvm-6dc is built and measured, but every measurement was taken on the test-bed
with nobody playing. One thing that cannot be measured that way:

A human takes seat one, and the switcher renumbers seats around whoever is
there. The seat a player holds is the seat the composition counts from, so a
lineup typed while somebody is on RED is the case with the most room to be
wrong and the least coverage.

What to check on a real server:

- swap a seat while a human is on RED and confirm the human keeps his place
- swap mid-wave and confirm it waits for the break rather than dropping
  buildings
- confirm the replacements come back with the money they had earned, which was
  measured with bots only
- !ap bots from a client, not rcon, since the menu path differs

Closing mvm-6dc on the build and leaving this open is the same shape as mvm-8ws
and mvm-15t: the work ships, the confirmation is its own bead.

title: The test-bed calls an install-time restart a crash
description:
run.sh ends with "the game server has crashed N time(s): that is a bug in what
is being measured, not a slow wave", and it gets N by counting "core dumped"
lines in the container log.

Most of those are not crashes in anything being measured. The test-bed installs
the mod and the statistics plugin and the server restarts around it, and every
one of those restarts leaves a "core dumped" line behind. They are all preceded
by "installed the bots and the statistics plugin".

It cost an evening. A reseat feature looked like it was crashing the server
across three runs, and the count was the only evidence. The one crash that
actually happened during play was the engine watchdog:

  [defenderbots] stuck: Waldo (engineer) ... for 12s, DefenderEngineerIdle
  WatchDog! Server took too long to process (probably infinite loop).
  FATAL ERROR: Host_Error: WatchdogHandler called - server exiting.

## What it should count instead

A crash that matters happens after the server has settled and while a wave is
being measured. Two things separate it from the noise:

- it is not preceded by the install line
- it carries a cause worth printing, and the two seen so far are
  WatchdogHandler and a plain segfault with neither

So: count crashes only after the "watching for N wave results" mark, and print
the WatchDog line when there is one, because "crashed 1 time(s)" and "the
watchdog killed it after an engineer was stuck for 12s" send you to completely
different places.
close_reason: Filed on a wrong inference. I thought the crash count included install-time restarts because each 'core dumped' was preceded by 'installed the bots and the statistics plugin'; that line prints every thirty seconds for the whole run, so it separates nothing. run.sh already scopes the count to this run's window and was right. What it could still do is print the cause, and that is worth having: 'crashed 1 time(s)' and 'the watchdog killed it after an engineer was stuck 12s' send you to different places. Refiled as that, narrowly.

title: A taunting bot holds the wave instead of readying
description:
Reported from a nightly run: a bot in a taunt animation does not press F4, and
the wave waits on it.

## Cause

`SetPlayerReady` announces readiness with a client command:

    FakeClientCommand(client, "tournament_player_readystate %d", state)

A taunt holds that. Because the command only goes out while the flag disagrees,
it is reissued every frame until it lands, so a short taunt merely delays the
ready and nobody notices.

A looping taunt does not end on its own. Then the command never lands, the flag
never flips, and the team sits at the ready screen waiting on a bot doing a
dance with no way to see which bot or why.

## Fix

`ReadyDefender` wraps the readiness calls in `UpdateDefenderReadiness` and ends
the taunt before saying ready:

    if (state && TF2_IsPlayerInCondition(actor, TFCond_Taunting))
        TF2_RemoveCondition(actor, TFCond_Taunting);

Only when readying, never when un-readying, so nothing cancels a taunt during a
wave. Between rounds a taunt is worth nothing to anybody, so it loses to the
ready rather than the other way round.

This is correct whether or not the engine was the thing refusing the command. If
the taunt was blocking it, this unblocks it. If something else was, a bot that
is not taunting is one fewer thing between the wave and starting.

## Not verified against a looping taunt

The reasoning above is from the code, not from a reproduction. Worth confirming
with a bot on a looping taunt that the wave now starts, since that is the case
that turns a delay into a hang. Bot taunts come from the loadout slots in
`util.sp` (`TF_LOADOUT_SLOT_TAUNT` and the two after it), so a config that gives
one is the way to set it up.
close_reason: Fixed. ReadyDefender ends TFCond_Taunting before setting ready, only on the readying path. Not reproduced against a looping taunt, which is the case that turns a delay into a hang; noted in the bead.

title: The teleporter exit is built inside the blast that kills the sentry
description:
Reported from a nightly run on Decoy: the engineers put their sentry beside
their teleporters, which reads as bad placement to anybody watching.

It is not a placement failure. It is the design, and the mod's own constants say
why it is wrong.

## The numbers already in the repo

`source/redbots3/behavior/engineerbuildteleporter.sp` anchors the exit to the
nest, and says plainly what the nest is:

    /* The exit stands off the nest centre rather than on it
       The nest centre is where the sentry is ... */
    #define TELEPORTER_EXIT_RADIUS  150.0

So the exit is always 150 units from the sentry, deliberately. Meanwhile
`source/redbots3/util.sp`:

    #define BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE  400.0

150 is well inside 400. The mod knows how far a sentry buster reaches, uses that
number to make bots run away, and then parks the teleporter exit at less than
half of it from the thing busters are sent to kill.

One buster takes the sentry and the exit together, every time. So does a giant
demo's spam or a tank's path. The engineer's whole investment sits in one blast
radius, and the team loses its forward spawn at exactly the moment the sentry
falls, which is when they most need to get back.

## Why the radius is that small

The comment explains the constraint it was solving, and it is a real one: eight
stand points aimed at the nest centre are eight looks at the sentry and eight
refused placements, so the spot walks around the nest and the engineer stands
between the two. 150 is "far enough out not to be inside his own sentry".

That is a build-validity radius, not a tactical one. It answers "where can he
physically place it" and never asks "where should it be".

## What to change

Separate the two questions. The exit needs its own spot chosen for survival and
usefulness, with the nest as a hint rather than an anchor:

- Outside `BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE` of the sentry. That single rule is most of the
  fix and the constant already exists.
- Still close enough to the fight that arriving players are useful, and still
  reachable, which is what the existing stand-point walk is good at.
- Not on the robots' path, or the exit is destroyed on the way past.

The map configs already support a hand-placed answer. Decoy declares
`TeleporterExit` at `-361 -159 573` while its nests are at `292 598 544`,
`214 537 364` and `-218 737 360`, so the configured exit is nowhere near a nest.
Check whether that configured spot is being used at all, because a run that
builds 150 units off the nest is not using it.

The Decoy config also declares no `TeleporterEntrance` at all: its
`Config_LoadMap` line reads `0 tele-in, 1 tele-out`. The entrance falls back to
stepping 200 units out of the spawn door toward the nest, which is why an
entrance can end up beside a nest that happens to sit near spawn. Whether the
entrance wants a configured spot per map is the smaller half of this.

## Test

The testbed already walks nests. Add a check that no teleporter is built within
`BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE` of a friendly sentry, and run it on Decoy and Coal Town.
That is the regression test and the acceptance test at once.
close_reason: Fixed in e20deb3. The exit now tries a ring at BUSTER_BLAST_RANGE + 100 all the way round before falling back to the old 150-unit ring, so a cramped map still gets an exit rather than none. Root cause was narrower than the bead said: Decoy names one TeleporterExit spot and NearestFreeExitSpot hands it to the first engineer, so with two engineers the second finds it taken, returns false, and drops to the nest-anchored fallback. That fallback was the unsafe path.

title: Bots look like they ready up but the ready does not register
description:
vixon2: "they sound like they're readying up but it doesn't go through"

Came out of Jebby asking how to stop the autofill bots auto-readying after each

title: Engineers do not replace a destroyed dispenser
description:
Cowser, in a list of bot suggestions: engineers should "always prioritize
replacing the Dispenser when it is broken".

Filed as a report, not a confirmed defect: he asked for it as behaviour rather
than saying he watched one fail to rebuild.
close_reason:
Measured rather than assumed, and it is mostly already what he asks for. Across every run in results/, 1441 stretches of an engineer alive inside a wave with no dispenser of his own: median 20 seconds, quartiles 10 to 25, which is the time it takes him to walk over and build one. So he does prioritise it.

The tail is real though: 58 stretches over a minute and a worst of 165 seconds. The cause is in the code rather than in the measurement - the dispenser branch in CTFBotMvMEngineerIdle_Update only fires when m_ctSentrySafe is in the future, so on a wave where the sentry is under fire continuously he never gets a window and the dispenser stays down for the rest of it. That is a defensible order, the sentry is the nest, and it is also exactly the wave where the team would want the dispenser.

Closing as measured. If it should change, the change is that gate and the number to hold it against is the tail above, not the median.

title: A refused purchase ended the whole shopping trip
description:
Forty five shopping trips measured on Bavarian Botbash: ten of them ended because
the game refused a purchase, and one of those walked away with 700 credits still
in the wallet. The reasoning in the code was that the ranking would pick the same
line again and be refused until the window ran out, which is true and is an
argument for remembering the refusal rather than for giving up on the trip.

`m_bRefusedUpgrade` is per trip. A refused line is skipped for the rest of it and
the next interval picks the next thing down. Upgrade steps a wave are unchanged
at a median of 17, which is what should happen: the trips that were ending early
now spend what they had left.

The exit reason is logged either way:

    [tf2_defenderbots.smx] Shopping: <name> stopped, <why>, <n> credits left
close_reason: Fixed in a87d742: the refusal is remembered for the trip and the next interval picks the next line down. Upgrade steps a wave unchanged at a median of 17.

title: The medic's patient
description:
`PreferredPatient` in `nextbot_behavior.sp` works out who the medigun should be
on: the most maximum health, which names the Heavy without a class table and
follows the health upgrades the team buys. `behavior/medicheal.sp` acts on it by
doing the healing itself rather than by arguing with the game's own action.

Writing the patient into the game's action is still off, and the reason is worth
keeping: `action.SetHandleEntity(ACTION_HEAL_PATIENT_OFFSET, ...)` segfaulted the
server on the first Mannhattan run, with no watchdog line, which is a memory
fault rather than a slow frame. The offset is a hardcoded field inside one of the
game's own actions. Everything else in this mod only reads it, and the difference
matters: reading a wrong offset gives a wrong answer, writing one corrupts
whatever is really there.

What was reported and is fixed: the medic stood in the house in the middle of
Coaltown for a whole wave. The candidate list was the team within nine metres, so
once the Heavy walked out of that the ask came back with the engineer at his nest
and could never come back with anybody else. The list is the whole team now, a
healthy engineer is not on it because his own dispenser is doing that job, and
the answer is held between asks because the gate that decides whether the medic
heals at all runs every frame and every ask is a path computation per teammate.

What is still open is where he should stand once he has a patient. He follows the
patient, and nothing in this mod says where the team holds, which is the same gap
item 3 records for nest scoring.

human actually reads is a teammate walking against the flow of the team, one
who never shoots at anything, and one whose class is not in a lineup the bots

That last one is nearly free here, because the mod picks the RED team and knows

title: Nothing senses which way the robots came
description:
The nest scorer reasons about the bomb and about static mesh data. `BOMB_DROP`,
nav visibility, the spawn room flags and `bot_hint_sentrygun` are all baked at
map compile time and identical every wave. The only dynamic inputs are the
bomb's position, which resets to the same place each wave, and `BLOCKED`, which
is now read.

So on a map where the mesh does not change and only the spawn door differs,
`ShouldRelocateNest` computes a gain near zero and correctly does nothing.
Mannworks is exactly that map, and it is where the note asking for this was
written.

The cheap way in is to watch the robots instead of the map. Sample live BLU
players on a timer, map each to a nav area, count visits per area, and use
"where robots actually walked" as the approach sample in place of the radius
around the bomb, falling back to today's sample when the count is empty. It is
one wave behind by construction: wave N is chosen from wave N-1's traffic,
which is right whenever the spawn side repeats and wrong exactly once when it
flips.

Parsing the popfile would know the route before the wave instead of after. It
is a text parser for a format with no schema, plus a file location problem on
custom missions, for information that arrives one wave later for free.

title: Nothing deploys the Medic's Projectile Shield
description:
Every guide puts one tick of it first for a Medic and they are right about a
person: it is the strongest single thing a Medic does to a wave. It is deployed
with the special attack key, and no behaviour in this mod has ever pressed one.

So `generate rage on heal` was three hundred credits at the top of the Medic's
list buying a meter that fills a button nobody uses. It is refused in
`IsUpgradeWasted` until something presses it, and the moment something does it
goes straight back to the top.

The wider point is worth keeping: the wiki is written for people, and a
recommendation is only worth copying where this mod's bots can do the thing it
assumes. Three of them failed that test in one pass. The Pyro's Destroy
Projectiles is an airblast the Phlogistinator has not got. Jump height reaches
credits a person can see on a ledge, and a bot walks where the nav mesh says.
And this one.

The two that passed are worth naming too, because the test is not "distrust the
guide": the Sniper really does aim at the head bone, so Explosive Headshot earns
its place at the top, and the Engineer's own play-tested ordering beat the page.

Imported from TODO.md item 6b — section: Behaviour and map data
Original heading: Nothing deploys the Medic's Projectile Shield. Open
close_reason:
Implemented and measured. The button is pressed now: MedicProjectileShield puts the shield up when the rage meter is full and something is shooting near his patient, and generate rage on heal is no longer refused in IsUpgradeWasted when the feature is on. It fires 26 to 35 times a run, logged, so a null result cannot be mistaken for a behaviour that never ran.

Three arms against the 24 attempt baseline on Bavarian Botbash wave 1: held 176s/58 robots, 240s/83, and 175s/60, against a baseline of 160s and 58 with quartiles of 154-192 and 52-64. The middle arm is outside the band on both and did not replicate, and the first shared the machine with another server. Two of three sit inside the band.

So it ships off, behind medic_shield, and the item's own premise is settled: the wiki is right that a person should press it, and this mod can now press it. Whether it is worth three hundred credits is what the switch is for.

comments.author: m-this
comments.text: Reopened the decision, not the issue: shipping on. Three arms could not tell it apart from the baseline, and the reason to keep it anyway is one the bed cannot measure - every run here is bots alone, and a shield between a robot's rockets and a human player is worth something none of these numbers count. medic_shield defaults on now.

title: A nest is scored for the bomb and not for the team

with bodies in front of it. A nest nobody passes is an engineer alone. Distance
to where the team holds belongs in that score, and the reason it is not there
yet is that nothing in this mod says where the team holds.

title: The Demoman is the weakest seat, and it is in every lineup
description:
A sweep of every map put it at 1634 damage a wave across forty waves, against
the Heavy's 8594, with a seat in all seven lineups.

It is not aim. 308 damage a kill is better than the Pyro's 354 and the Heavy's
425: it is efficient with what it fires and does not fire enough.

Holding the launcher by default was tried and measured and it is worse. Six
waves of Coaltown either way, one build, one switch between them:

| | damage a wave | kills | cleared |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pipes first | 1821 | 27 | 5 of 6 |
| stickies first | 880 | 11 | 4 of 6 |

Half the damage, so the switch is gone rather than left off. The hole in the
argument was that the bot fires at where a robot is rather than where it is
going: a sticky thrown at a walking robot lands behind it and catches nobody,
and the clip and the reload are spent for nothing where a pipe at least does its
damage when it connects.

Which leaves the trap, and the trap is the thing the guides are actually
describing when they say a Demoman's damage is in his secondary. Bombs go on
ground the robots have not reached yet, and the bot waits. `behavior/stickytrap.sp`
lays one, and it only ever runs when no threat is visible at all, on a twenty
second cooldown, so during a wave it never runs. That gate is the next thing to
move, and it wants measuring the same way this was.

Two smaller things went in alongside and are unmeasured, because they were in
both arms: a Medic is always worth the switch to the launcher, and detonation is
counted across the whole cluster rather than answered by the first bomb that
qualifies.
